html:
DOCUMENTATION AND ANALYSIS OF PRIOR SOLUTION ATTEMPT

Real World Technology

Our team looked at seismic bracing as a technology that could potentially reduce the risk of damage to our building during earthquakes. This technology involves installing support systems that can absorb and dissipate seismic energy, increasing the structural integrity of the building. There are many types of seismic bracing configurations, including cross-bracing, buckling-restrained braces, V-braces, and suspended zipper column braces. Each configuration offers unique advantages and can be tailored to the specific needs of the building. There are many examples of these techniques being used in the real world, such as in skyscrapers in earthquake-prone regions like Japan and California. We specifically researched the One Maritime Plaza in San Francisco, CA.

This building utilizes a structural steel framework consisting of two grids of 5- story high cross braces stacked atop one another. These bracing systems provide lateral stability by resisting horizontal forces generated during an earthquake. Some types of braces are designed as a fuse for the building during an earthquake. Earthquake forces attack the weakest link, and in this case, they are the braces. These braces are designed to absorb the energy from the earthquake, protecting the rest of the building from damage.

Relevance of Prior Solutions to Design Challenge

After our research, we decided that seismic bracing is the best earthquake resistant technology for our model building. We have a budget of $700,000, and we want something that is relatively easy to place on our building’s facade. Seismic braces absorb and distribute energy, preventing excessive swaying and maintaining stability. They are strategically positioned within the building’s structural framework to ensure effective load transfer. It strikes a balance between structural performance and cost, making it a viable option for most building types. We specifically chose V-bracing as it is a lot easier to fasten on the exterior compared to other types of bracing systems. We do not need to spend as much time and effort perfecting each measurement.

Research Sources

We looked at many places when researching seismic bracing techniques. These included websites developed for building design and technology. Architects and engineers all over the world use sites like the Whole Building Design Guide to gather information on the latest advancements in structural engineering. This allowed us to make an informed decision on the most suitable bracing system for our project.

PROTOTYPE TESTING AND DATA COLLECTION PLAN

Building Modifications Chosen:

· Two large middle beams

· “V” bracing

· Cross-bracing or additional skeletal beams

These modifications were chosen primarily based on their perceived effectiveness in improving earthquake resistance. After conducting research on specific earthquake resistant techniques, we were able to produce these three modifications that we believe will significantly enhance the building’s ability to withstand seismic activity. The two middle beams were chosen to be the structural core of our building. Most high-rise buildings have this to help support the weight of the building. We chose this to ensure maximum stability and structural integrity during earthquakes, as the core beams may play a crucial role in distributing forces and minimizing sway. In the case of V-bracing, we selected it due to its capability to provide lateral support and reduce the building’s vulnerability to horizontal movement during an earthquake. Cross-bracing is remarkably similar, and it is used in many real-world structures for the same purpose of enhancing stability and reducing the risk of collapse during seismic events.

Exclusions From Testing

Other techniques were excluded from testing because they were too complex and unproven for our small testing setup. Viscous dampers, which could have gone overbudget, would be overly complex to design and install in our original 12-story base case.

Other teams were putting in pendulums, which are essentially mass dampers. These solutions are effective in reducing the impact of seismic events on tall buildings, but they were not feasible for our testing purposes. It is important to consider cost, complexity, and practicality when choosing seismic retrofitting techniques for a specific structure.

Planning Testing

We split the testing for each modification into three separate phases. Phase one is conducted with one test per speed level of a shaker table, which simulates earthquakes. Phase two follows the same approach as phase one, but phase three includes three tests per speed level to capture a wide range of data under varying conditions, improving data reliability and accuracy.

The test plan had some up sides, like taking a close look at distinctive designs to see how tweaks affect the building’s resistance to earthquakes. We ramped up testing slowly, going from one test per level to three in phase three, which helped us verify our data and fine-tune the results for the different techniques. Collaborating with other teams and sharing results also made for a great collaborative vibe and gave us a chance to cross-check our findings. However, this method of testing did come with its own drawbacks. A few trials may not have revealed all the strengths and weaknesses of each modification, which can be discovered through more thorough testing. Furthermore, human error could occur due to weight misplacement or insufficient balancing. If the building were too heavy, it would cause the motor to slow down and thus lead to skewed results.

TESTING, DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS

Data Collected and Performance Metrics

We as a class collected a lot of data on how each modification of the base building behaved when it was put through the earthquake simulations.

This involved taking measurements of the structures’ movement and their reactions to various stress levels. We then assessed which designs could withstand the most amount of shaking and maintain stability, and now we could tell which modifications worked well and which did not. We also examined how the buildings performed when extra weight, such as snow, was applied to them to simulate real-world conditions.

We also collected key metrics, which we could use to compare our specific modifications to the base building and other teams’ data. These comprised the peak acceleration and the resonance frequency. To evaluate the building’s response to seismic activity, the resonant frequency is crucial. This resonant frequency, at which the building shakes the most, can tell you what magnitudes will cause the most damage to a building. The simulation tool collects the frequency for every test, and using that, we can find where the resonance occurs. The peak acceleration measures the maximum amount of acceleration or shaking the building experiences during the simulation. This is measured using the accelerometers that plug into the shaker table set.

Data Analysis

Our test results from phase two show that the two core beams did a lot better than the base structure. The data shows that the resonance occurred at 2.1 Hz. The peak acceleration for the building without snow was around 0.314 g, which was not particularly different from the base structure, which had an acceleration of 0.355 g. Our team’s design did a lot better than other designs in terms of structural stability during the simulation. As you can see, designs like the pendulum had a much higher peak acceleration, making them less stable under added weight at the top compared to our design. However, we saw that seismic bracing techniques only had a peak acceleration of about 0.291 g. As we researched, this design was effective in minimizing peak acceleration by dissipating the horizontal forces in simulated seismic conditions. The results indicate that our modifications were pretty successful in improving the building’s resilience to external forces. In conclusion, this class data suggests that implementing seismic bracing techniques can significantly enhance structural stability in buildings subjected to seismic conditions.

Factors Affecting Data Accuracy and Interpretation

There are a few sources of variability and potential errors in our data collection and analysis process that must affect how we interpret the results. Along with the errors discussed in the test plan, one major issue we as a team ran into was the inconsistency of our motor. Sometimes it did not run at the speed we needed, so the seismic spectra looked kind of wonky. That makes it hard to get accurate data. We risk making mistakes in our reasoning or misinterpreting our results if we analyze this data without taking those factors into consideration. So, we have got to be careful when we look at the data and keep these issues in mind.

CONSTRUCTION OF A TESTABLE PROTOTYPE

When making our final model, we aimed to pay close diligence. Our goal is not to have a design that falls flat because we failed to consider a minor but significant detail. Not only does the structure need to be visually beautiful, but it also needs to be structurally strong and earthquake resistant. We followed a detailed construction plan, maintaining strict standards to ensure that the finished model met our testing expectations.

We chose V-braces as the main structural element in our final design. These braces span multiple levels, significantly increasing the building’s ability to withstand large shakes. We planned to have the V-braces placed in a way that they circle around the building. Our final design didn’t cost much as it was everything in the base structure plus medium sizes beams. These are supposed to be strong and rigid as they will take most of the force caused during the simulation.

Final Design Dimensioned Diagrams: The units where every grid square is equal to 2 centimeters.

Final Design Costs and Materials:

Construction Process

For constructing this, we used hot glue, balsa wood beams (both large and medium), a sheet of foamcore, utility knives for cutting, and rulers and pencils for measuring things.

We started off by making the base case of the 12-story building. We cut out the four large beams, so each of them is 72 inches in length.

These were the frames that provided the necessary support for the building. Additionally, we carefully measured out and drew notches every six centimeters on the large beams, as that is where the floors of the building would be attached. Side by side, we marked the locations for the cuts on the 14 cm by 14 cm foamcore base. We did this by making four marks four cm away from the corners of our foundation and we cut the corners from those marks we made. The foamcore base was now octagonal and we drew two lines between the edges. We also sketched the design of the rectangular building supports on the same foamcore. We cut the supports out and set them aside so that when we get our final building done, we could glue them on.

We used cardboard cereal boxes to cut out 12 six cm by six cm squares as the floors. We also remembered to cut out the small 0.6 cm x 0.6 cm squares on each floor’s edges, which are crucial for sliding the large beams through.

As we were using V-braces for our earthquake-resistant concept, we had to cut out Vs from the medium beams. Each half of the “V” measured 12.5 cm. We first marked these lengths on all four medium beams before cutting them out. There were exactly 24 cut out beams which gave us enough material for 12 usable Vs. We set these aside so we could assemble the main structure of the building.

Before gluing anything, we had to mark the direction of the cardboard’s grain. This step is crucial for the building’s stability. We did this by just drawing an arrow pointing which way the grain is going.

Before gluing anything, we had to mark the direction of the cardboard’s grain. This step is crucial for the building’s stability. We did this by just drawing an arrow pointing which way the grain is going. One by one, we hot glued the floors to two of the large beams, making sure that they were precisely positioned on the latches. We alternated the placement of each of the floors so that the grain goes vertically and then horizontally. We made sure to glue that 12th floor on one of the ends of the beam.

Once all 12 floors were attached to the first two frames, we repeated the process with the other two, taking care to align the smaller cuts on the floor’s edges with the latches.

Finally, it came down to gluing the 12 V-braces around the building. As mentioned in our plan, we couldn’t cover the entire building’s facade with braces. This was due to the budget and the fact that more braces could mean more error in the construction. So, instead of doing that we stuck to our plan of alternating the sides of the two floors where the Vs would go.

We used this same approach until we had to put the braces on the bottom two floors. Here, we ended up shifting one “V” up a floor to keep stability at the base. Lastly, we glued the final structure to the base by placing the building’s four large beams in the middle of the octagonal base. Then, we glued the supports in a pinwheel-like form around the building.

Difference Between Model and Actual Build

Our building mostly followed the original plan, but we had to make adjustments for stability. In a real build, these adjustments would likely be unnecessary due to stronger materials and construction techniques. Some included re-gluing a few of the braces as they would snap. The biggest problem we had in building our specific structure had nothing to do with the plan at all. Hot gluing together the beams and supports was a challenge, as the glue would often dry too quickly before we could properly align the pieces. This resulted in some sections being less secure than we would have liked.

CONSIDERATION OF DESIGN VIABILITY

V-braces ensure that the power of a quake passes smoothly down to the base, reducing weak points that may fail when things get nasty. They act as the fuse in an earthquake, absorbing the shock and preventing damage to the overall structure. In addition to all the technological benefits, these braces seem pretty cool, too. They let us throw in some creative design touches on the outside without messing with the building’s safety or how well it works.

The V-bracing worked well for phase three, as our team’s peak acceleration was only in the 0.1s. For the building without snow, the resonant frequency was 2.0 Hz, as expected. However, as the snow adds more weight at the top, the building sways more, and thus, the resonant frequency was 1.3 Hz. This building would be considered safe for the most part. If you looked really closely at the building while testing, you could notice some smaller tremors. But for the most part, looking at it from a distance, the building appeared stable and secure during the simulation. However, we encountered a few problems with our motor during the testing of the snow. As a result, our frequencies and accelerations were pretty low. The acceleration was lower with snow on the top of the building than without it because the added weight at the top, combined with the strong base and the V-brace reinforced middle, created a balanced structure.

Our final design tower most definitely met the requirements and constraints set forth by the clients. The peak acceleration was more than 0.2 g lower than that of the baseline data. Our design almost eliminated any form of swaying or shaking. Although resonance occurred at 0.2 Hz, which aligns with the frequency of earthquakes in the area, the acceleration was too low to have any significant impact. The class decided a building would be defined as “safe” when the acceleration was between 0.18 and 0.34 g. Our team’s acceleration was significantly lower, measuring 0.17 and 0.14 g for the no-snow and snow tests, respectively. The final building met all constraints, including a minimum height of 12 stories, and we completed it with nearly $60,000 left in our budget.

The building boasts notable strengths, including a tremendously low peak acceleration, well below baseline data, and an unconventional spiral arrangement of braces ensuring stability from all sides. Its simplicity and adaptability to most building facades, combined with the project’s $60,000 cost savings, highlight its economic and structural benefits. However, weaknesses in the design were also identified, notably the fragility of the V-brace medium beam, which raised concerns about potential breakage under stress, leading to vibrations that could compromise the building’s interior integrity.

Additionally, the necessity of adopting a spiral brace pattern, primarily driven by budget constraints, deviated from our preference for a more uniform distribution. These observations highlight areas for potential enhancement in both the construction and design phases. For example, incorporating notches into the major beams could provide a more tailored fit for the V-braces, reducing reliance on adhesive and lowering the risk of breakage due to uneven surfaces. The design process revealed a missed opportunity to fully utilize V-braces, despite significant budget flexibility, because their placement lacked a carefully planned pattern. This underscores the need for us to adopt a more calculated approach to distributing braces to fully leverage available structural and financial resources.

CITATIONS

title: Launching Dreams: My Rocketry Journey
excerpt: A few days ago, my rocketry team and I headed out to 60 Acres Park in King County, Washington. It marked our final launch day for the qualifying launches for the American Rocketry Challenge. The typical Seattle…
html:
A few days ago, my rocketry team and I headed out to 60 Acres Park in King County, Washington. It marked our final launch day for the qualifying launches for the American Rocketry Challenge. The typical Seattle clouds dotted the sky, with occasional glimpses of the sun and minimal wind, providing ideal conditions for launching our rockets without any hitches. With each countdown — 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 — we eagerly watched as our rockets soared into the sky, leaving behind trails of smoke accompanied by a distinct whooshing sound. As each rocket reached its apex, we collectively held our breath, hoping for a successful flight and landing. Upon opening the nose cone and checking the altimeter post-parachute deployment, we were astonished by the readings: 841 feet with a flight duration of 44.3 seconds.

The Start

When I joined the rocketry club at my high school, I didn’t know what to expect. I was just there because a few of my friends from middle school had joined it, and I wanted to try something new. Little did I know that launching rockets would become such a complex yet super fun and competitive hobby. At Tesla STEM High School, our rocketry club participates in TARC, The American Rocketry Challenge, which is the world’s largest rocket contest, with nearly 5,000 students nationwide competing each year. High school students can design, construct, and launch model rockets as part of the competition, which also provides them with practical experience in problem-solving engineering.

The American Rocketry Challenge | World's Largest Student Rocket Contest

Teams that qualify for the American Rocketry Challenge National Finals have the chance to win cash prizes. This is what really got me hooked, and it was the fact that you could go to nationals just if your team got a max height of around 820 feet and your rocket came down with an uncracked egg in 45 seconds.

After all the planning and registration, we reached the purchasing stage. Here, we had to meticulously choose the materials and components for our rocket to ensure it met the competition standards. Being fairly new to model rockets, our team initially made several errors in purchasing the wrong parts. Yet, with some guidance and research, we managed to rectify these mistakes, refining our design before the test launch.

Starting to Test

However, we did make two big catastrophic errors in what components we bought. We bought a really powerful F50T-6 Aerotech motor and a really big 36 cm parachute, and our first test launch went a whopping 1200 feet in the air. The top body tube that held the egg tore off from the rest of the rocket when the parachute went up. As it came crashing down, the parachute kept floating away so far that we couldn’t even retrieve it. This was our first big mistake that we learned from and made sure to avoid in future launches. Despite the setback, we were able to salvage the project and make improvements for a successful launch next time.

TEST 1 FOR TARC

The Final Launches

Then the date approached for the final qualification launch, which consisted of three separate launches that would all be compiled together for a final score. We persevered through many struggles in this launch, including trying to get our egg out of the top tube and making sure we had an altimeter. But yet , despite the challenges, our team managed to successfully complete all three launches and achieve a high final score.

Launch 1: 848 feet in 45 seconds

Launch 2: 841 feet in 44 seconds

Launch 3: 857 feet in 39 seconds

The competition only takes the best two of our three launches, and for time, we were on the dot. However, for height, we were about 20 feet off. But most teams that get this kind of score go to nationals, and that got us pretty excited.

TARC Qualification Launch 1

The fact that a first-timer who barely knew anything about rockets could achieve such results was truly impressive. We were proud of our hard work and dedication, which paid off in the end. This experience taught me the importance of teamwork, adaptability, and persistence in the face of adversity in rocketry projects. The sense of accomplishment and camaraderie we felt were truly rewarding.

Thank you for reading!

title: Engineer You World Pinhole Camera: Technical Report
excerpt: A simple camera made with materials found in an art studio for people with disabilities enrolled in the arts program.
html:
1. The Need

A simple camera made with materials found in an art studio for people with disabilities enrolled in the arts program.

2. User Needs and Constraints

Engineering is when a societal need is met using math, science, and technology. In our case we have the art studio for people with disabilities. These people need a camera to take photos of a 10 ft x 10 ft mural outside their art studio. The entire mural must fit into a 4 in x 5 in sheet of film paper and the image shouldn’t be too small or too big. They have limited range hand dexterity which is like a pair of oven mittens on your hands. So, the camera should be easy to grasp. The materials also need to be inexpensive and mostly be things that can already be found in the art studio. Finally, the pinhole camera must go along with a set of instructions on how to use it. While using the camera, the person must stand at least 5ft away from the mural. However, the courtyard in front of the art studio is only 20 ft x 20 ft. This makes for at most 15 ft of moving space. The problem of adapting a large mural onto a small sheet of film paper is solved via an aperture. It’s the small hole in the front of any camera letting a diffused amount of light in. These light rays bounce off the object that you are pointing at and directly enter through the aperture. If you move closer to the mural, the bigger the image will be on the film. The farther back you move, the smaller your image. Nonetheless, there are other factors that determine how your image will look like how long the focal length-the length between the aperture and the film. We take in a lot of elements like the distance between the camera and mural, the height of the mural and width of the film to get a variable distance of 2–8 inches.

3. Initial Concept Generation

Before going to the actual mind map and brainstorming various aspects of our camera, we had to find a suitable body for our camera. I decided to bring a shoebox as it was the exact height for the film paper. It was also structurally sound, and we could do many things with it without it deteriorating in capability. However, when you use a shoebox, it could be too wobbly for a person with hand dexterity to use. We started thinking about making a handle of some sort to easily solve this problem. Next, we did the flashlight test by putting some sort of light inside our box with the lid closed. We took the box to a darkroom as then we could see all the leaks in our box. We mostly had leaks in the corners and the sides where the lid closed. We decided for our camera that we need to fill these areas up so no light can be let in, and the picture comes out perfectly. When we looked at other people’s Light leak test results, we found that most of them were cardboard boxes with a few minor leaks that could be readily repaired.

We first used sticky note brainstorming, which is basically to develop ideas quickly that meet a couple of needs on the camera. Such items include film paper stuck inside rectangular cardboard holders or a big handle on top of the aperture. The sticky note brainstorming helped us visualize these ideas and arrange them in a logical manner on our mind map later. We were able to generate and organize innovative concepts for our camera design more efficiently by using this method. My partner and I took these sticky notes and organized them into groups, with each group having ideas that met separate demands in the camera.

In our mind map, we put these ideas into groups. The plus side of having many ideas is that they allow us to find problems in some and adapt others. Additionally, this systematic approach enables us to brainstorm more effectively, as we can explore different angles and perspectives within each group. We analyzed each group to identify common themes and prioritize the most feasible ideas. This turned into our sliding mechanism later on. This process assisted us in narrowing our options and developing a comprehensive plan for improving the camera’s functionality.

Concept A — One of the concepts we developed was the aperture cover. We considered a sealing piece of cardboard that would flip and close the aperture. The discussion about this turned into an idea that would be beneficial to our camera later on. It was the slide-in mechanism in which the cover or holder would slide between two cardboard rails. This slide-in mechanism would not only provide a secure closure for the aperture but also allow for easy and quick access when needed.

Concept B — We thought of another concept with that slide-in mechanism employed, but this time it was for the film paper. More specifically, the job of securing it. We imagined a sliding tray into which you would insert the film, like a photo frame, except that the photo had not yet been taken. The slide-in tray would enter through a small inlet on the side of the shoebox, as the cover of the box would be completely taped shut.

Concept C — Another interesting concept we explored was for any camera opening, mostly for taking out and putting in the film. We thought of two large doors or flaps on any side of the box. This allows us to use our hands to get in the box and secure the film.

Design From C-sketch

We didn’t choose an exact C sketch as different people from other groups put things onto our initial idea. Instead, we looked though all the drawings to see which ones might fit our project well. After careful consideration, we finally decided to combine elements from various sketches that aligned with our project’s goals. This collaborative approach allowed us to incorporate diverse perspectives and create a unique and cohesive C sketch. We came up with two main elements that are beneficial to our design. This was the aperture cover and the film holder. For our aperture cover we used the slide in technique already outlined in the mind map section. However, we did add some extra things from people’s drawings on our c-sketches like a handle attached to the aperture cover so that you can easily pull it. For our film holder we got a few ideas from the C-sketching that just visualized what we were going to do. Although most of the C-sketches had us opening an entire side of the box, they also offered some solid suggestions for protecting the film. One of these is to add a photo frame-like structure to hold the film. So, I decided that merging both concepts would be beneficial because we now have a dependable film holder and a secure piece of film.

4. Prototype Building

At first, we analyzed materials and made a mistake about the focal length of their film box. We decided to decrease the focal length by an inch by moving the back wall of the box forward. The next day we created a pinhole punch for the aperture using a sewing needle and an aluminum square. We also made a design change to use magnets instead of sliders or an inlet. We spray painted the interior of the box black to reduce light leaks. The aperture cover was then constructed using cardboard rails and black foam core. The aperture cover was completed with a handle and the photo frame part of the film holder. We also created a pull tab attachment for the little entrance on the box’s side. Our camera’s core skeleton was completed.

Description of Build

On the first day, we began by analyzing all our materials and figuring out what we needed to do first. But then we realized we’d made a huge mistake, and it had to do with our focal length. It was longer than 8 inches, therefore our image wouldn’t be able to fill the entire film. So, we decided to reduce the focal length of the box by about an inch by “shifting” the back wall forward. We hot glued and taped a 12" x 5" piece of cardboard to a specific position, reducing the focal length of our box to roughly 7 inches. On day two we made the pinhole punch for the aperture. The pinhole punch was created using a sewing needle and a 2"x2" aluminum square. The square was pressed into the square, creating a dimple, and sanded off. A 1"x1" square was cut in the middle of the front of a box, and our aluminum square was taped to the inside. On day three, we made a design change in which instead of having sliders or a small inlet to secure the film holder at the back of our box, we could use magnets to hold our film holder to the back of the box. However, one of our magnets got lost, and we had to scrap this idea. I also started working on the actual film holder with the photo frame-like style. On day four, we spray painted the whole interior of the box black to allow less light to bounce around and ruin a beautiful photo. I discovered that hot gluing the top of our film holder to the photo frame was a bad idea because it deteriorated every time, we placed it into our inlet. A hot glued film holder was simple to make repairs since you could add more and more, and it would keep working. This was not a sustainable long-term solution. After this we started building the aperture cover which sits on “rails”, two long pieces of cardboard.

The actual cover will be a piece of black foam core fastened in between those two pieces and an extra two on top to hold it in place. On day five we completed the aperture cover finished with a handle that tells you if it is closed or opened. I finished working on the photo frame part of the film holder and now we started making the pull tab attachment that you must insert into the small inlet on the side of our box. On day six we finished the pull tab and patched up the box as much as possible for the coming development test. The barebones for our camera to work was done.

Initial Results

For our first development test, we went to the darkroom and inserted the blank film into our holder. We closed our entire box and took it outside for light to get in through any possible inlets that there might be. After some time, we took it back into the light room and started doing the development process. By putting the film into several types of liquid chemicals. Our Test strip (above) came out pretty dark mostly because the carboard is not fully light proof. That really black spot could be the small openings near the inlet for our film holder.

Modifications

After that, we decided that because the box isn’t completely light proof, we should wrap it in aluminum foil. It will reduce the amount of light coming in.I ultimately chose to add some Velcro to the top and sides of the film holder. We also placed a black waste bag measuring 60 cm × 60 cm over it. We put aside the aperture closure and film holder while wrapping it in aluminum foil because you had to hide those with smaller items. After these modifications we did our second development test and the strip came out completely white, meaning there was no light penetration. We first took a picture of a gate about 10 ft long and had trees in the background. (see below)

However, our exposure time was only 306 seconds, four times our calculated exposure time on a day with dense cloud cover. The picture came out mostly white even if you invert it, you only see some outline of trees in the background. We probably need to adjust our exposure time based on these results.

Subsequent Testing

The next day we took another picture but kept the times 4 on our exposure time as it was a sunny day. This time we were taking a picture of a fire hydrant. The picture still came out exceptionally light even if used the same exposure time on a sunnier day! Finally, we realized that there was probably something wrong with our aperture itself. When we re-measured it, it came out as 0.3 mm; this was quite different than that of the 0.4 mm we measured when we cut out our pinhole on day two. Because of this, we had redone our exposure time calculations.

Final Product

We took a photo of the front of a school bus for our final image. Considering it was a cloudy day, we quadrupled the exposure duration to 8 minutes and 8 seconds. Even after all of this, our image turned out whiter than we expected. Even though the markings on the school bus may be seen, the genuine bus cannot be completely replicated on film paper. We thought the reason for this could be the lightness of yellow and how it is harder to capture with only so much time. Other than the actual picture, our camera met all the requirements of our client. It captured a 10 ft x 10 ft object. It could be used by people with hand dexterity, as we tested it out with oven mittens. It was also very inexpensive, as all our materials were things you could find in an art center.

5. Final Representation

For our final report that we give to the user, we gave all the building instructions in a numbered list. We also gave instructions to use the camera. This document had all the critical product specifications which include the aperture size of 3 mm, the film size 10.16 cm x 12.7 cm, the focal length 17.15 cm, and our base exposure time of 127 seconds. We also gave the user all the tools and the exact sum of each of the materials used in the build. After looking through these resources our client, the art studio and its members can successfully build and use a pinhole camera.

6. Reflection

Looking back, this project turned out to be an exciting engineering challenge. We worked through each of the steps in our engineering design process, researching and finding user needs, then doing an analysis to designing, prototype building, testing, and finally, the retrospection. We went through multiple rounds of designing, testing, and working together to solve problems to meet the unique requirements of our customers who struggle with hand dexterity. Reflecting on the project we learned useful lessons from the mistakes and difficulties with communication we met. One notable occurrence was when we had issues with the film holder. Our first design did not adequately block light, resulting in leaks. This proved the importance of being willing to change your original design when things don’t go as planned. As a result, we quickly reinforced the weak points by integrating more materials. This small tweak made our design more light-tight, pointing out the importance of being able to adapt on the fly for the success of the project. Additionally, we met communication issues during the prototype building phase. Due to unclear communication about the design, my teammate and I had differing ideas on constructing the aperture cover. This made us see the need for better communication between us, a lesson learned for next time. Overall, the project broadened my understanding of how engineers work. It made visible the effects of well-executed design.
